cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.

context_blocks.text: Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.

cards.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
cards.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most \(Cn(\log (n+2))^{a}\) bits of memory and \(C(\log (n+2))^{b}\) passes, with success probability at least \(2/3\) for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set \([n], n\ge 2\), with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous \(O(n \log ^{a}(n+2))\)-bit space and \(O(\log ^{b}(n+2))\)-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
cards.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

importance.reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most \(n- 1\) scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc \((u,v)\) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) passes require \(n^{2- o(1)}\) space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the \(\Omega (\log  n/\log  \log  n)\) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\) as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

cards.title: Perfect matching in NC
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,a,b>0\) and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most \(C(n+2)^{a}\) gates and depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{b}\)?
cards.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
cards.definitions: The input is the \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix of a graph on \([n]\), with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an \(n\times n\) binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\), fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the \(n^{2}\) output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input \(1^{n}\) writes the description using \(O(\log _{2}(n+2))\) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

cards.status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits \(n^{O(\log ^{2} n)}\) processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. cards.definitions: There are \(n\ge 2\) bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in \([n^{2}]\); shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability \(2^{1- k}\). Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability \((1- p)^{n}\), which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition \(p\cdot d^{c}<1/2\) is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form \(O(d/\log  d + (\log  \log  n)^{O(1)})\) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an \(O(\log  \log _{1/p} n)\) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same \(O(\log  \log  n)\) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in \(O(\log  n)\) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The \(\sqrt{n}\) term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)\). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound \(\tilde\{O\}(\sqrt{n} D^{1/4}+D)\), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra \(D^{1/4}\) factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+\sqrt{n}+D)\), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For \(D\approx n^{1/2}\), its displayed terms give \(n^{3/5+o(1)}\), while the target is \(\tilde\{O\}(n^{1/2})\). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires \(n^{3/5}\) rounds.

The notation \(n^{o(1)}\) allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as \(n^{b+1}\), forcing exactness by taking \(\varepsilon\) extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its \(\varepsilon\) dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.

cards.definitions: For each \(n\ge 2\), the communication network is the complete graph on processors \(1,\ldots ,n\). The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the \(n- 1\) adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with \(\mathrm{P}(G)\) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. \(R_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement \(R_{A}(n)=\omega (1)\) means that for every integer \(B\ge 1\) there is N such that \(R_{A}(n)>B\) for every \(n\ge N\); it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the \(\omega (1)\) target.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed \(\omega (1)\) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The network and the input graph differ
context_blocks.text: Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

context_blocks.title: One bit can be much easier than collecting the input
context_blocks.text: For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

context_blocks.title: Why unicast is essential
context_blocks.text: In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

context_blocks.title: The explicitness requirement
context_blocks.text: Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

context_blocks.title: Connections and known limitations
context_blocks.text: The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an \(\Omega (\log  \log  n)\) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker \(\omega (1)\) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.

cards.title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized parallel algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in any directed graph with integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots,n^{a}\}\), using \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Output integral arc flows. Use a synchronous priority CRCW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed; if several processors write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes one word-RAM instruction per round, with the instructions and word length specified below. Work is the total number of executed processor instructions, including activation, input access and output; depth is the number of rounds. Processor IDs and addresses fit in words. All processors run a fixed finite program with their IDs; there is no advice or free preprocessing. Independent uniform random words cost one instruction each. The entire output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Both resource bounds hold on every execution. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. With \(N=m+n\), require a function \(h_{a}:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h_{a}(N)/\log N=0\), such that work is at most \(C_{a}Nh_{a}(N)\) and depth at most \(C_{a}h_{a}(N)\). The program, \(d\), \(C_{a}\) and \(h_{a}\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph. Initially the explicit input is in shared memory; all subsequent computation is charged.

cards.title: Work-efficient parallel directed reachability
cards.formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
cards.why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
cards.definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density.

Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.

context_blocks.text: A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”

cards.formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? cards.why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) the input is the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The output is a parent array \(p\in \{0,\ldots ,n\}^{n}\), with 0 denoting a root. If \(p(v)\ne 0\), require \(\{v,p(v)\}\in E(G)\); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each circuit \(C_{n}\) has \(n^{2}\) input bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most \(O(n^{c})\) and depth at most \(O((\log _{2}(n+2))^{k})\), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given \(1^{n}\), writes the description of \(C_{n}\) while using \(O(\log (n+2))\) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.

sentences: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration.
For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.

cards.context:
Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge \(\{2,3\}\) joins different branches. The path with parent pointers \(p(1)=0, p(2)=1\) and \(p(3)=2\) is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height \(n- 1\), yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m+n)\) and depth \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{n})\), where m is the number of edges and \(\widetilde{O}\) suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.

cards.title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log * n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every \(n\ge 3\) and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least \(1- 1/n\) in $T(n)=o(1+\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from \([n^{2}]\), and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.
cards.definitions: The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |\(0\rangle\) ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |\(0\rangle\) registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in \(\{1,2,3\}\). Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. \(T(n)\) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is \(T(n)/(1+\log * n)\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty ; \log\)* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.
cards.why: This is a canonical test of quantum advantage for a natural distributed symmetry-breaking task. A faster protocol would improve one of the basic local coordination primitives; a lower bound would have to explain a limitation of quantum realizability that mere causal consistency does not capture.

importance.reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.

progress.text: Cole–Vishkin and subsequent algorithms give \(O(\log * n)\) classical coloring. Linial proves a matching deterministic lower bound. These classical bounds also give a quantum upper bound by running a classical protocol.

context_blocks.text: A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is \(\Theta (\log * n)\).

Naor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs \(\Omega (\log * n)\) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.

There is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.

The August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.

A separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.

cards.formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.

progress.text: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$.

Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier.

Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?

cards.title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint \((n/2)\)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is \(O(n)\) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
cards.definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.

context_blocks.text: Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.

cards.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be \(O(\log  n)\) uniformly over degrees.

context_blocks.text: Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal simulation, including the time, memory and arbitrary-tree guarantees. Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. A slow merge procedure with short messages, a separation using a promise, or a private-randomness separation does not decide this specified question.

context_blocks.text: The workshop page asks broadly whether good streaming algorithms yield good sketches and compares one-way with simultaneous communication. Editorial specialization: this card selects the deterministic, total-function question with efficient merging. Feldman, Muthukrishnan, Sidiropoulos, Stein and Svitkina show that symmetric deterministic streaming computation can be distributed through a binary aggregation tree with comparable message size and polynomially related space. Their simulation uses reachability search and can take superpolynomial time. The retained target asks whether that time cost can always be avoided.

A sequential chain of merges is itself a streaming computation. The converse must support balanced trees and every other arrangement, even when the stream algorithm’s intermediate states record order-dependent information that disappears from the final answer.

The cited paper also gives failures of analogous comparisons for promises, multiple permissible outputs and private randomness. This card removes those routes to a separation by requiring a total Boolean function and deterministic exact computation. The malformed final sentence on the workshop page is not used as a theorem statement.

Associativity of the summary representation is not required: two different trees can leave different internal summaries provided both decode correctly. Demanding identical summaries would strengthen the problem beyond the aggregation model used here.

Recent turnstile-to-linear-sketch simulations address algebraic update streams and space preservation. Their hypotheses and conclusions do not provide this uniform polylogarithmic-time merging theorem for arbitrary insertion streams and arbitrary total symmetric functions.

cards.title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(n\ge3\), is there a deterministic linearizable wait-free implementation of an unbounded FIFO queue for \(n\) asynchronous processes using only atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set objects?
cards.definitions: Processes have distinct identifiers, arbitrary private memory and no timing information. The shared primitives are atomic registers supporting Read and Write of finite values, and test-and-set bits initially zero: TAS returns the old bit and sets it to one. An unbounded supply of fresh primitives is permitted; stronger atomic operations are not. Each process can repeatedly invoke either Enqueue(v), for any finite binary string \(v\), or Dequeue(). Sequential queue semantics append at the tail, remove and return the oldest item at the head, and return a distinguished empty marker immediately when empty. Linearizability requires each concurrent history to admit a sequential ordering of completed operations and a subset of pending operations that obeys these semantics and respects real-time precedence of nonoverlapping operations. Wait-freedom requires every operation of a process that continues taking steps to complete after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of delays or crashes of others. There is no restriction to designated enqueuers or dequeuers and no bound on the number of operations. Algorithms may depend on \(n\); they receive no random coins.
cards.why: The queue question tests whether consensus number alone captures the strength of basic concurrent data types, and whether weak primitives can provide per-process progress.

cards.title: Deterministic volume gap
cards.formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with \(V_{A}(n)=o(n)\) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with \(V_{B}(n)=O(1+\log * n)\)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots ,|V(G)|^{2}\}\). Here \(V_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed \(\Delta \ge 2, a\) fixed verification radius \(r\ge 1\), finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, \(\Pi\) and the exact |\(V(G)|\), and visited set \(\{v\}\). It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. \(\log * n\) is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no \(O(\log * n)\)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every \(C>0\) and every \(n_{0}\), some \(n\ge n_{0}\) satisfies \(V_{B}(n)>C(1+\log * n)\). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
cards.why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) can be sped up to deterministic \(O(\log * n)\). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL.
Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above \(\log * n\) remains the issue here.
Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear.

Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity \(\Theta (\log ^{k} n)\) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.

context_blocks.text: A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the following decision problem in logspace-uniform NC? An input gives positive integers W,H, an explicit W-by-H array c with entries in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), and two cells p,q in that rectangle. Extend c by zero to the whole integer square lattice and add one grain at p. Answer YES exactly when q eventually topples under the four-neighbor parallel sandpile dynamics defined below. The input length N includes every array entry, not a compressed representation.
cards.definitions: The four neighbor displacements are \(E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\}\). Set \(c_{0}(v)=c(v)+1\) if \(v=p\), and \(c_{0}(v)=c(v)\) otherwise. At each integer time \(t\ge 0\) every vertex v with \(c_{t}(v)\ge 4\) topples once, losing four grains and sending one to each neighbor. Equivalently, \(c_{t+1}(v)=c_{t}(v)-4 I[c_{t}(v)\ge 4]+\sum\)_{e in E} \(I[c_{t}(v-e)\ge 4]\), where I is the indicator. The question is whether \(c_{t}(q)\ge 4\) for some \(t\ge 0\). The array is row-major with binary dimensions and cell coordinates; invalid encodings are rejected. The zero extension is an infinite lattice, not a periodic boundary or a boundary that absorbs grains. A supplied rectangle may contain extra zero rows or columns to include p and q. Finite initial mass eventually stabilizes. NC here means that for some fixed integers a,k the decision has Boolean circuits of size \(O(N^{a})\) and depth \(O((\log  N)^{k})\), with fan-in at most two, whose description is generated from \(1^{N}\) in \(O(\log  N)\) work space. There is no requested time t in the input and the answer is exact, without random error.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute membership of the specified language in logspace-uniform NC. Any complexity assumption used in a negative result must be stated explicitly.
cards.why: A local deterministic physical process can have a long cascade after a single perturbation. This problem asks whether its outcome permits an efficient parallel computation, addressing the boundary between prediction and sequential evolution.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.

context_blocks.text: The initial configuration is stable, so all activity comes from the extra grain. The requested output is a single eventual-toppling bit; computing the entire final configuration or a toppling at a specified time are related but different tasks.
The classical dimension-dependent results provide efficient parallel prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three. They leave the planar case as a distinct question.

Recent work still separates the standard four-neighbor lattice from weighted or nonuniform grids. NC membership and P-completeness are not an unconditional exclusive dichotomy: a P-completeness result rules out NC only under \(\mathrm{NC} \ne  \mathrm{P}\).

cards.title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
cards.formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. Equivalently, determine the classification function \(\chi(\phi)\in\{0,1\}\), equal to one exactly for functions with such algorithms.
cards.why: A full classification would explain which local comparisons of large frequency vectors retain enough structure for accurate compression under deletions. It would connect individual distance estimators and impossibility results through a general mathematical criterion, including dissimilarities that are not norms or even metrics.

sentences: A local nonnegative cost φ defines a dissimilarity by summing over corresponding frequency coordinates.
The stream may insert and delete frequencies while keeping both vectors nonnegative.
The selected task classifies exactly which effectively evaluable costs admit polylogarithmic-space relative approximations.
The criterion must cover the entire specified domain and include both algorithms and impossibility proofs.
Known offset obstructions, difference-based aggregate classifications and norm-sketching results cover only parts of this domain.

cards.definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.
